rationale: Group-relative methods standardise rewards within a rollout group, so what reaches the optimiser is the relative spacing of rewards and not their values. Two consequences follow and both are measured. A linear rescaling of the reward is cancelled by the normalisation and changes nothing, while a bounded nonlinear reshaping survives it -- which is why replacing an unbounded error gap with a reciprocal mapping matters: an unbounded reward lets one outlier rollout inflate the group standard deviation and compress the advantages of every near-optimal sibling toward each other, so the group stops distinguishing better from best exactly where the useful gradient is. The direct comparison is the sharpest evidence: standard group-relative training given that reciprocal mapping beats four published optimisation-level variants -- reward normalisation, sample filtering, sequence-level ratios, soft advantages -- each run with the naive unbounded reward. That comparison is deliberately asymmetric, as its authors state, so it establishes that the two kinds of fix are not interchangeable rather than that reward-level fixes dominate. Three further sources give the same asymmetry from other directions. A derivation of what the normalisation optimises shows the induced prompt weighting under binary rewards is one over the square root of p(1-p), diverging at both ends, with the realised waste measured at 36.4 percent of one benchmark's token-level gradient budget spent on prompts already above a 0.9 pass rate -- a property of the reward-to-advantage transform that no optimiser change addresses. A reward-granularity sweep under fixed optimisation settings is monotone from sparse to hierarchical to argument-factorised, while the same paper finds token-level weighting improving the group-relative method and severely destabilising a batch-normalised one, so a shaping choice cannot be evaluated apart from the optimiser it is fed to. And a rubric study finds a reward-shape change -- grading each criterion correct, missing or wrong rather than yes/no -- worth 2.25 points of medical macro-average while an optimiser-side intervention on the same system moves that average by 0.25. The counterweight, and the reason this is stated as an asymmetry rather than a ranking, is that a difficulty-dependent multiplier interacts badly with the same normalisation and weakens a penalty precisely where outcome variance is highest: reshaping the reward is powerful because the normalisation transmits it, which also means a poorly chosen shape is transmitted.
statement: Under group-relative optimisation the shape of the reward is a more effective lever than the optimiser, because the normalisation cancels a linear rescaling and preserves a nonlinear one — so fixing a sparse or badly-scaled signal at the reward is not interchangeable with fixing it at the update rule, and the two must be compared before either is credited.
